claims.text: GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev's confidence-scored decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the past week.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
In GeoDeploy's design, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing, and does all the math, but never makes judgment calls.
In GeoDeploy's design, Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use, but never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names.
In GeoDeploy's design, Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS, but never decides anything.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost for each candidate.

GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules including EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
The Pulumi Automation API runs a preview and then an update, with one stack per region, in GeoDeploy.
GeoDeploy's Automation API run won't execute at all unless the user's cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md file with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives: choice(), score(), and noul().
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric the caller describes, and GeoDeploy uses 10 levels for its rubrics.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only ever selects from closed sets and never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region ID or a made-up Pulumi argument can't happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates, along with the constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

In a single call, GeoDeploy asks Jev for a region selection, five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, and architecture consistency), two hard checks (data residency satisfied and sufficient capacity), and a fallback region choice.
The options passed to choice() are the priced candidates themselves, keyed by ID, so Jev cannot answer with a region that isn't on the list.
TypeSafe advises rubric authors to "describe situations, not degrees" when writing score() rubrics.

GeoDeploy's coverage rubric uses 10 levels, ranging from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" up to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."
The five scores in GeoDeploy feed a ranking system that runs on weight profiles: latency-optimized (the default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
GeoDeploy's "latency-optimized" weight profile uses cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, and archConsistency 0.12.
GeoDeploy's "balanced" weight profile uses cost 0.25, coverage 0.25, maturity 0.2, sprawl 0.12, and archConsistency 0.18.
GeoDeploy's "residency-first" weight profile uses cost 0.12, coverage 0.12, maturity 0.38, sprawl 0.23, and archConsistency 0.15.
GeoDeploy's "failure-domain" weight profile uses cost 0.08, coverage 0.17, maturity 0.48, sprawl 0.15, and archConsistency 0.12.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider, such that AWS always means EKS and ECR.
Jev is left to make judgment calls on ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier in GeoDeploy.
GeoDeploy checks every Jev answer against a confidence threshold matched to how risky the decision is.
In GeoDeploy, a data-residency decision requires a confidence threshold of 0.95, and failing that results in a hard reject.
In GeoDeploy, a region decision for a new cluster requires a confidence threshold of 0.90, and failing that flags the top three candidates for a human to choose.
In GeoDeploy, a region decision when a stack already exists requires a confidence threshold of 0.75, and failing that keeps the existing region.
In GeoDeploy, an ingress or autoscaling module decision requires a confidence threshold of 0.85, and failing that uses the registry default.
In GeoDeploy, a node-pool sizing tier decision requires a confidence threshold of 0.60, and failing that uses the bin-packing result.
In GeoDeploy, the global floor confidence threshold for region pick, residency, or capacity decisions is 0.50, and falling below it drops the AI path for that geo.
Each AiPathAborted error in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so even a rejected answer ends up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or returns an error, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing the residency and constraint checks.
Running `geodeploy explain` shows why each region won.

When GeoDeploy's self-driving mode is enabled via `geodeploy monitor`, the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, code (not Jev) computes the actual node-count changes.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, a resize is applied automatically above 0.85 confidence.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, a resize is suggested for human approval between 0.70 and 0.85 confidence.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, below 0.70 confidence GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.

CPU utilization alone is described as a poor autoscaling metric, and is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency or error rates once a traffic baseline is established.
Users need access to Jev and a cloud provider to get started with GeoDeploy today.
GeoDeploy's source code is hosted on GitHub at pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
The Pulumi Automation API is documented at /docs/iac/automation-api/.
TypeSafe Jev is documented at https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.
